status: drafted via multi-agent workflow, adversarially fact-checked and corrected
notes: Acts is the largest, most character-dense narrative book indexed so far after Genesis — 28 chapters covering roughly three decades, structured in the two halves the guidance names: a Peter-centered Jerusalem/Judea/Samaria phase (ch 1-12) and a Paul-centered Gentile-mission phase (ch 13-28), hinged on Cornelius's conversion (ch 10) as the theological turning point. No law/theme tiers were used — unlike Leviticus or Deuteronomy, Acts has no content-heavy instructional sections; even its long speeches (Peter's Pentecost sermon, Stephen's defense, Paul's Areopagus/Felix/Agrippa speeches) are personally embodied moments within a manager's own narrative arc, not detached teaching blocks, so they're logged as verse entries under the speaker rather than spun into separate law tiers. No standalone 'Jesus' tier was created (he ascends in Acts 1 before the narrative proper begins) — his one appearance, to Saul on the Damascus road (9:3-9), is logged as a verse entry on Paul's own tier per the book-specific guidance, not a new character. Two tiers were promoted past the Matthew precedent's scale: Silas earned his own major tier (not just 'Paul's companion') because he has real, personally-embodied scenes distinct from Paul's — the Philippi beating, imprisonment, and midnight hymn-singing are his ordeal too, not just backdrop to Paul's — and Herod Agrippa II earned his own tier separately from his great-uncle Herod the Great (Matthew) and his father Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12), since two full chapters (25-26) center on his personal judgment of Paul's case and his own famous reply. By the same promotion test, Ananias of Damascus (9:10-19) was deliberately NOT promoted to his own tier despite a genuinely personally-embodied scene (named individually, receives a vision, voices real fear, then obeys and physically restores Paul's sight) — the distinguishing factor from Cornelius (whose conversion is the book's own stated theological hinge, spanning three full chapters of doctrinal weight) and Apollos (who recurs independently across three separate chapters, Ephesus through Corinth) is that Ananias's action, however vivid, is confined to a single episode that exists to serve Paul's own arc rather than carrying independent narrative weight of its own; this is a judgment call under rule 3, not a mechanical outcome, and is flagged here rather than left silent. Paul's tier accumulates by far the most submanagers (17) of any tier indexed to date, which is a faithful reflection of the text, not an invented list — roughly two-thirds of Acts (9, 13-28) is built around his journeys, trials, and the dozens of officials, converts, and companions he meets along the way, rather than an artifact of over-indexing; this count now includes Ananias the high priest (23:2, 24:1), a real accusing presence at Paul's trial, and Aristarchus, a Thessalonian companion with independent textual presence across three separate scenes (19:29, 20:4, 27:2) exceeding several already-indexed single-scene submanagers such as Eutychus or Publius. Several genuine naming collisions recur across this book and must never be silently merged: four men named Herod (Agrippa I here, Agrippa II here, plus Herod the Great and Herod Antipas already indexed in Matthew); at least three, arguably four, men named Simon — the book's own central manager tier, Simon Peter, alongside Simon the sorcerer under Philip's tier, Simon the tanner (Peter's Joppa host, folded into Peter's own verses with no independent action), and Simon called Zelotes, named only in the Acts 1:13 apostle roster with no further action and logged below as a named entry; two named James (James of Jerusalem, presiding at the Jerusalem council, vs. James son of Zebedee, executed by Agrippa I — plus a third, James son of Alphaeus, named only in the Acts 1:13 apostle roster with no independent action); three named Ananias (Ananias of Damascus, who restores Paul's sight; Ananias the husband of Sapphira; and Ananias the high priest, who orders Paul struck at his hearing before the council (23:2) and formally accuses him before Felix (24:1) — a real, distinct third figure now indexed as a submanager under Paul's tier); a third, previously-unflagged 'John' among the high priestly kindred present at Peter and John's own Sanhedrin hearing (Acts 4:6) — distinct from John son of Zebedee and John Mark, though he takes no independent action and stays in genealogyLists rather than the character list; and three named Judas (Iscariot, whose death Acts 1:18-19 describes independently of and with different physical detail than Matthew 27:5 — logged descriptively without attempting to reconcile the two accounts, per the project's non-interpretive rule; Judas of the street called Straight in Damascus, a pure address marker folded into genealogyLists; and Judas surnamed Barsabas, a real co-actor alongside Silas, indexed as his submanager). A further naming variance, short of a full collision since neither figure has independent action beyond being named, is flagged rather than silently resolved: 'Gaius... of Macedonia,' caught alongside Aristarchus in the Ephesus riot (19:29), and 'Gaius of Derbe,' listed in the Asia travel company (20:4), carry different location descriptors within Acts's own text, suggesting two possibly-different men sharing the name — kept as a flagged, unresolved genealogyLists entry rather than merged. Several figures who are traditionally assumed to be relatives of major characters — James of Jerusalem as "the Lord's brother," Bernice as Agrippa II's sister, and Herod Agrippa II's own descent from Herod the Great — are flagged in funFacts as coming from outside Acts itself (Galatians/1 Corinthians for James; general secular history via Josephus for Bernice and for the Agrippa II/Herod the Great lineage) rather than asserted as something the text of Acts itself states. A number of named-but-undifferentiated groups (the Antioch prophets/teachers of 13:1 beyond Barnabas and Saul, the sons of Sceva, the remaining Acts 20:4 travel-companion list — now limited to Sopater, Secundus, Gaius, and Tychicus, since Timothy, Trophimus, and Aristarchus are each indexed individually — the Sanhedrin members of 4:6, Tertullus, Theudas and Judas of Galilee, and the unnamed Egyptian of 21:38) are kept out of the character list entirely and logged in genealogyLists instead, since the text does not differentiate their individual actions.

characters.name: Simon Peter

verses.note: Leads the church in choosing Matthias to replace Judas among the twelve.
Preaches at Pentecost; about three thousand souls added that day.
Heals a man lame from birth at the temple's Beautiful gate, with John.
Arrested with John, testifies before the Sanhedrin, 'we cannot but speak.'
Confronts Ananias and Sapphira over their lie to the Holy Ghost; both die.
Imprisoned with the apostles, freed by an angel, testifies before the council again.
Heals Aeneas at Lydda; raises Dorcas from the dead at Joppa; lodges with Simon a tanner.
Sees the vision of the sheet with unclean animals; preaches to Cornelius's household as the Holy Ghost falls on Gentiles.
Imprisoned by Herod Agrippa I, freed by an angel, comes to Mary's house where Rhoda answers the door.
Speaks at the Jerusalem council, affirming salvation by grace for Gentile believers.

funFacts: Naming-collision flag: Peter lodges with 'Simon a tanner' (Acts 9:43, 10:6) — a different man entirely from Simon the sorcerer under Philip's tier; folded here rather than given his own entry since the text shows him no independent action beyond hosting.
Acts itself never restates Peter's father's name; Matthew 16:17 calls him 'Simon Bar-jona' (son of Jonas), but that detail is outside this book's own text.

characters.name: John (son of Zebedee)
characters.perkNote: Naming-collision flag: this is John son of Zebedee, one of the twelve — distinct from John Mark (Barnabas's tier), from the unnamed 'John' of the high priestly kindred at Acts 4:6 (kept in genealogyLists), and from any later John (e.g. the traditional authorship question around Revelation, out of this book's scope).

genealogy.father: zebedee — Matthew 4:21, not individually indexed in Acts

verses.note: Goes to the temple with Peter; present at the healing of the lame man.
Arrested and examined alongside Peter before the Sanhedrin.
Sent with Peter to Samaria; they lay hands on believers to receive the Holy Ghost.

funFacts: His brother James (son of Zebedee) is indexed separately below as a named entry, executed by Herod Agrippa I in Acts 12:2.

characters.name: Matthias

verses.note: Put forward alongside Joseph called Barsabas; chosen by lot to replace Judas among the twelve.

funFacts: Qualified per Peter's own criterion: a man who had companied with the apostles 'all the time' from John's baptism to the ascension (1:21-22).

characters.name: Mary, the mother of John Mark

verses.note: Her house is where 'many were gathered together praying' the night the angel frees Peter.

funFacts: Her home functioning as a gathering place implies real means and standing in the early Jerusalem church, though the text states this only implicitly.

characters.name: Ananias and Sapphira
characters.perkNote: Naming-collision flag: this Ananias is distinct from Ananias of Damascus (Acts 9) and from Ananias the high priest (Acts 23-24) — three separate men sharing this name across the book, indexed separately under Peter's and Paul's tiers.

spouses: each other, a married couple — Acts 5:1

verses.note: Ananias sells land, keeps back part of the price, lies to Peter about it, and dies.
Sapphira, unaware, repeats the same lie about the price and dies as well.

funFacts: Kept as one collective entry, since the text gives them one mirrored act (the lie, the price, the death) rather than two independently differentiated storylines.

characters.name: Gamaliel

verses.note: A Pharisee and doctor of the law, 'had in reputation among all the people,' advises the council to leave the apostles alone, citing Theudas and Judas of Galilee as cautionary precedent.

funFacts: His counsel directly spares the apostles a harsher sentence, functionally reducing the 'cost' of the trial to Peter's tier without Gamaliel ever becoming a believer himself in the text.

characters.name: Rhoda

verses.note: A damsel who answers the gate when Peter knocks; too glad to open it, she runs to report he's there instead, and isn't believed.

funFacts: Described as a 'damsel' (young servant girl) in Mary's household.

characters.name: Dorcas (Tabitha)

verses.note: A disciple at Joppa 'full of good works and almsdeeds'; dies, is mourned by widows showing coats she made, and is raised by Peter.

funFacts: Her name is given in both Aramaic (Tabitha) and Greek (Dorcas) by the text itself, both meaning 'gazelle.'

characters.name: Simon called Zelotes

verses.note: Named among the eleven remaining apostles gathered in the upper room; given no further individual action in this book.

funFacts: Naming-collision flag: at least three, arguably four, men named Simon appear across Acts's own text — this Simon (called Zelotes, one of the twelve), Simon Peter (this book's own central manager), Simon the sorcerer (indexed under Philip's tier), and Simon the tanner (Peter's Joppa host, folded into Peter's verses with no independent action) — none of them the same person.

characters.name: Stephen

verses.note: Chosen as one of the seven to serve, described as 'full of faith and of the Holy Ghost.'
Does great wonders among the people; opponents in the synagogue of the Libertines are unable to resist his wisdom.
Falsely accused of blasphemy before the council; his face seen 'as it had been the face of an angel.'
Delivers his defense, retelling Israel's history from Abraham through Solomon, ending by rebuking his accusers.
Stoned to death; sees the heavens opened and the Son of man standing at God's right hand; prays for his killers as Saul looks on.

funFacts: The first Christian martyr recorded in scripture; his death directly precedes and provokes the great persecution that scatters the church (Acts 8:1).

characters.name: Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas

verses.note: Named alongside Stephen and Philip as the seven chosen to serve tables; Nicolas is specified as 'a proselyte of Antioch.'

funFacts: Kept as one collective entry — the text names all five but gives none of them individual action beyond the appointment itself, unlike Stephen and Philip.

characters.name: Philip the Evangelist

children: four unnamed daughters, virgins, which did prophesy — Acts 21:9, not individually indexed

verses.note: Chosen as one of the seven deacons.
Preaches Christ in a city of Samaria; great joy results as unclean spirits and the sick are healed.
Simon the sorcerer believes his preaching and is baptized.
Led by an angel to the Gaza road; explains Isaiah's prophecy to an Ethiopian eunuch and baptizes him.
Caught away by the Spirit, found preaching from Azotus onward to Caesarea.
Now called 'Philip the evangelist,' hosts Paul at Caesarea; his four daughters prophesy.

funFacts: Naming-collision flag: this is Philip 'the evangelist,' one of the seven deacons — distinct from Philip the Apostle, listed only in the roster of the twelve (Acts 1:13) with no further action in this book.

characters.name: Simon the Sorcerer
characters.perkNote: Naming-collision flag: distinct from Simon Peter, from Simon the tanner (Peter's Joppa host), and from Simon called Zelotes, one of the twelve apostles (Acts 1:13, indexed above as a named entry).

verses.note: Had bewitched Samaria with sorcery, claiming to be 'some great one'; believes Philip's preaching and is baptized.
Offers Peter and John money to buy the power to bestow the Holy Ghost; is sharply rebuked by Peter and asks for prayer.

funFacts: His attempt to purchase spiritual power gave rise to the later term 'simony.'

characters.name: The Ethiopian Eunuch

verses.note: A man of Ethiopia, an officer of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, returning from worship at Jerusalem, reading Isaiah.
Asks Philip who the prophet means, is taught of Jesus, requests baptism, and goes on his way rejoicing.

funFacts: Left deliberately unnamed by the text; no later Acts-internal reference names him, so no name is asserted here.

characters.name: Barnabas

verses.note: A Levite of Cyprus named Joses, sells land and lays the money at the apostles' feet; surnamed Barnabas, 'son of consolation.'
Takes the newly-converted Saul and brings him to the apostles, vouching for him when the church is afraid of him.
Sent to Antioch, exhorts the new believers there, described as 'a good man, full of the Holy Ghost and of faith.'
Goes to Tarsus to fetch Saul, and together they teach the church at Antioch for a year.
Set apart with Saul for missionary work by the Holy Ghost at Antioch.
Mistaken for the god Jupiter by the crowd at Lystra.
Attends the Jerusalem council; later has sharp contention with Paul over John Mark and sails for Cyprus with Mark instead.

funFacts: His original name, Joses, is stated directly by the text (4:36) alongside the surname the apostles gave him.

characters.name: John Mark

verses.note: His mother Mary's house is the prayer meeting Peter comes to; he is taken along by Barnabas and Saul from Jerusalem.
Attends Paul and Barnabas as their minister on Cyprus, then departs from them at Perga to return to Jerusalem.
Paul refuses to take him on the second journey because of his earlier departure; the disagreement causes Paul and Barnabas to part ways.

funFacts: Later epistles (Colossians 4:10) describe him as Barnabas's cousin — a detail outside Acts's own text, not asserted here as this book's fact.

characters.name: Saul / Paul the Apostle

verses.note: As Saul, keeps the clothes of Stephen's executioners and makes havoc of the church, dragging believers to prison.
Blinded by a light on the road to Damascus; hears the risen Christ's voice, 'Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?'
Ananias of Damascus restores his sight and he is baptized.
First called by the name 'Paul': 'Saul, (who also is called Paul).'
First missionary journey with Barnabas through Cyprus and Asia Minor.
Sees the vision of a man of Macedonia calling him over.
Preaches to the philosophers at the Areopagus in Athens on 'the unknown god.'
Seized in the temple at Jerusalem; a riot breaks out and he is arrested.
Shipwrecked en route to Rome after appealing to Caesar.
Bitten by a viper on Malta and shakes it off unharmed.
Spends two years in his own hired house in Rome, preaching the kingdom of God with all confidence, no man forbidding him.

funFacts: Acts 22:3 states he was born in Tarsus in Cilicia; Acts 23:6 that he was 'a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee'; Acts 22:28 that he was 'free born,' a Roman citizen by birth.
Acts 23:16 mentions 'Paul's sister's son,' who overhears and reports an ambush plot against him — neither the sister nor the nephew is named in the text.

characters.name: Ananias of Damascus
characters.perkNote: Naming-collision flag: distinct from Ananias the husband of Sapphira, indexed under Peter's tier above, and from Ananias the high priest (Acts 23:2, 24:1), a third distinct Ananias also indexed under this tier below.

verses.note: A disciple at Damascus, initially fearful, told in a vision to go to Saul.
Lays hands on Saul, restoring his sight; Saul is baptized and receives food.

funFacts: Also mentioned by Paul himself, recounting the same event, in Acts 22:12-16.

Not promoted to a full manager tier despite a personally-embodied scene — his action, however vivid, is confined to a single episode serving Paul's own arc rather than carrying independent narrative weight across the book, unlike Cornelius or Apollos; see the book notes for the full reasoning.

characters.name: Timothy

verses.note: A disciple at Lystra, son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father; Paul has him circumcised and takes him along.
Sent ahead with Silas while Paul goes to Athens.
Listed among Paul's traveling companions from Macedonia to Asia.

funFacts: Later epistles name his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois (2 Timothy 1:5) — a detail outside Acts itself; Acts describes his mother only as 'a certain woman, which was a Jewess, and believed.'

characters.name: Aquila and Priscilla

verses.note: Paul finds them at Corinth, recently come from Italy after Claudius commanded Jews to leave Rome; he lodges and works with them as tentmakers.
Sail with Paul to Syria; left at Ephesus.
Hear Apollos speak boldly in the synagogue and take him aside to expound the way of God more perfectly.

funFacts: Aquila is specifically identified as 'born in Pontus' (18:2).

characters.name: Elymas (Bar-jesus)

verses.note: A Jewish sorcerer and false prophet on Cyprus who withstands Paul and Barnabas, seeking to turn the proconsul from the faith; Paul strikes him blind.

funFacts: 'Elymas' is given by the text as the meaning of his name ('the sorcerer,' 13:8).

verses.note: The deputy (proconsul) of Cyprus, 'a prudent man,' who desires to hear the word of God and believes after seeing Elymas struck blind.
A silversmith who makes shrines for Diana of the Ephesians; incites fellow craftsmen against Paul's preaching, fearing loss of trade.
The resulting uproar fills the city's theatre with confused shouting until the townclerk quiets the crowd.
A young man who falls asleep during Paul's long sermon at Troas, falls from a third-story window and is taken up dead; Paul restores him alive.

characters.name: Publius

verses.note: The 'chief man of the island' of Malta, lodges the shipwrecked party three days; his father, sick of a fever and bloody flux, is healed by Paul.
Other diseased islanders come and are healed also; the party is honored with many gifts.

funFacts: His unnamed father's healing is the direct cause of the rest of the island coming for healing.

verses.note: A centurion of Augustus's band charged with delivering Paul to Rome; courteously lets him visit friends at Sidon.
Prevents the soldiers from killing the prisoners during the shipwreck, 'willing to save Paul.'

characters.name: Felix

verses.note: The governor before whom the high priest Ananias and the orator Tertullus accuse Paul; Paul answers for himself.
Sends for Paul with his wife Drusilla to hear him on faith in Christ; trembles as Paul reasons of righteousness, temperance, and judgment, but hopes for a bribe and leaves Paul bound two years.

funFacts: Drusilla is named as 'his wife, which was a Jewess' (24:24) but takes no independent action in the text, so is not given her own entry.

verses.note: Succeeds Felix as governor; before him Paul appeals to Caesar rather than be tried at Jerusalem.
Lays Paul's case before the visiting Herod Agrippa II, unsure what charge to send with him to Rome.
Deputy of Achaia; dismisses the Jews' accusation against Paul as a matter of their own law, and 'cared for none of those things' when Sosthenes is beaten before his judgment seat.

characters.name: Agabus

verses.note: A prophet who signifies by the Spirit that there should be a great dearth (famine) throughout the world, which comes to pass in Claudius's day.
Takes Paul's girdle, binds his own hands and feet, and prophesies Paul will be bound at Jerusalem and delivered to the Gentiles.

funFacts: The only Acts figure to prophesy by symbolic act rather than speech alone.

characters.name: Lydia of Thyatira

verses.note: A seller of purple of Thyatira, a worshipper of God at Philippi; the Lord opens her heart to attend to Paul's words, and she and her household are baptized.
Paul and Silas return to her house after their release from prison.

funFacts: Traditionally regarded as the first recorded convert in Europe, based on Philippi's location in Macedonia.

characters.name: Trophimus

verses.note: Listed among Paul's traveling companions, identified as 'of Asia.'
Jews from Asia, having seen him with Paul in the city, wrongly suppose Paul brought him into the temple — the accusation that sparks the riot leading to Paul's arrest.

funFacts: A minor companion whose mere presence with Paul directly triggers the riot and arrest that drive the rest of the book's plot.

characters.name: Aristarchus

verses.note: A Macedonian, Paul's companion in travel, seized alongside Gaius and dragged into the Ephesus theatre during the riot of the silversmiths.
Listed among Paul's company traveling into Asia, identified as one 'of the Thessalonians.'
Boards the ship to Rome with Paul, described as 'a Macedonian of Thessalonica,' one of the few named companions on the voyage.

funFacts: Present with Paul across three separate scenes spanning roughly a decade of narrative time (Ephesus, the Asia journey, and the voyage to Rome) — more independent textual presence than several other indexed single-scene submanagers such as Eutychus or Publius.

Naming note: the 'Gaius' seized alongside him at Ephesus (19:29) carries a different location descriptor ('of Macedonia') than the 'Gaius of Derbe' later listed in the same travel company (20:4) — flagged as a possible naming variance in genealogyLists rather than asserted as the same or different man.

characters.name: Ananias the High Priest
characters.perkNote: Naming-collision flag: a third, distinct Ananias in this book — separate from Ananias of Damascus (9:10-19, indexed above) and Ananias the husband of Sapphira (5:1-10, indexed under Peter's tier).

verses.note: Presiding as high priest at Paul's hearing before the council, commands those standing by to smite him on the mouth; Paul rebukes him, then apologizes on learning he is the high priest.
Comes down to Caesarea with the elders and the orator Tertullus to formally lay accusation against Paul before the governor Felix.

funFacts: Distinct from the earlier high priest Annas named at Acts 4:6; secular history (Josephus) identifies him as Ananias son of Nedebaeus, high priest circa AD 47-58 — a detail outside Acts's own text, not asserted here as this book's fact.

characters.name: Cornelius the Centurion

verses.note: A centurion of the Italian band at Caesarea, devout, feared God with all his house, gave much alms, prayed always; an angel tells him to send for Peter.
Awaits Peter with his kinsmen and near friends gathered together.
The Holy Ghost falls on him and his household as Peter speaks; they are baptized, the first recorded Gentile converts.
His conversion is defended by Peter before the Jerusalem church as evidence that God grants repentance unto life to the Gentiles also.

funFacts: His unnamed kinsmen and near friends are gathered but given no individual action, kept out of the character list per the collective-group rule.

characters.name: Herod (Agrippa I)

verses.note: Stretches forth his hand to vex certain of the church, and kills James (brother of John) with the sword.
Seeing it pleases the Jews, imprisons Peter also, intending to bring him forth after Easter; an angel frees Peter instead.
Gives a public oration; the people cry 'It is the voice of a god, and not of a man'; an angel of the Lord smites him because he gave not God the glory, and he is eaten of worms and dies.

funFacts: Naming-collision flag: called simply 'Herod' throughout Acts 12 — this is Herod Agrippa I, one of four men named Herod across this book's own scope (himself, his son Herod Agrippa II below, plus Herod the Great and Herod Antipas already indexed in Matthew). Secular history (Josephus) identifies him as a grandson of Herod the Great, but Acts itself states no such genealogy.

characters.name: James (son of Zebedee)

genealogy.father: zebedee — Matthew 4:21, not individually indexed in Acts

verses.note: Killed with the sword by Herod Agrippa I — his death is reported in a single verse, with no personal action of his own shown in this book.

funFacts: Naming-collision flag: brother of John (indexed under Peter's tier above) — distinct from James of Jerusalem and from James son of Alphaeus, named only in the apostle roster (Acts 1:13) with no further action.

characters.name: James of Jerusalem

verses.note: Peter, freed from prison, instructs the disciples to 'shew these things unto James, and to the brethren.'
Presides at the Jerusalem council, rendering the judgment that Gentile believers not be troubled with circumcision, only certain necessary abstentions.
Paul reports to James and the elders at Jerusalem; they advise him to join four men under a vow to quiet rumors about his teaching.

funFacts: Naming-collision flag: distinct from James son of Zebedee and James son of Alphaeus. Later epistles (Galatians 1:19, 1 Corinthians 15:7) identify a 'James, the Lord's brother' widely understood to be this same figure — but Acts itself never states that relationship, so it is flagged here as outside this book's own text, not asserted as Acts fact.

verses.note: A Jew born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, mighty in the scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord but knowing only the baptism of John; speaks boldly at Ephesus until Priscilla and Aquila expound the way of God to him more perfectly.
Helps the believers in Achaia much, mightily convincing the Jews publicly that Jesus was Christ.
Paul arrives at Ephesus while Apollos is at Corinth.

characters.name: Silas

verses.note: A chief man among the brethren, a prophet, sent with Judas Barsabas to carry the Jerusalem council's letter to Antioch.
Chosen by Paul to accompany him on the second missionary journey after the split with Barnabas.
Beaten with many stripes and cast into prison at Philippi alongside Paul.
Sings praises with Paul at midnight; an earthquake opens the prison doors and the jailor is converted.
Paul declares them both 'Romans' (Roman citizens), uncondemned and beaten publicly.
Travels with Paul through Thessalonica and Berea.
Rejoins Paul at Corinth, coming from Macedonia.

funFacts: Widely identified with 'Silvanus' named in 1 Thessalonians 1:1 and 1 Peter 5:12 — the same Greek name in a Latinized form — though Acts itself always calls him Silas.

characters.name: Judas surnamed Barsabas
characters.perkNote: Naming-collision flag: distinct from Judas Iscariot and from the Judas of Damascus mentioned only as an address marker in Acts 9:11.

verses.note: Chosen with Silas, chief men among the brethren, to carry the Jerusalem council's letter to Antioch and exhort the brethren, being prophets themselves.
Sent away in peace back to the apostles after his work at Antioch is done.

funFacts: Also a candidate to replace Judas Iscariot alongside Matthias, as 'Joseph called Barsabas' (Acts 1:23) — whether this is the same man as Judas Barsabas of chapter 15 is not stated by the text and is not asserted here.

characters.name: The Philippian Jailor

verses.note: Wakes to find the prison doors open after the earthquake and draws his sword to kill himself, supposing the prisoners fled, until Paul cries out that all are present.
Asks 'what must I do to be saved,' is told to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, washes their stripes, and is baptized with his whole household.

funFacts: Left unnamed by the text — called only 'the keeper of the prison.'

characters.name: Herod Agrippa II

verses.note: Arrives at Caesarea with Bernice to salute Festus; hears Festus lay out the perplexing case against Paul and says, 'I would also hear the man myself.'
Paul is brought before him and Bernice 'with great pomp,' so Festus can have a charge to send with him to Rome.
Gives Paul leave to speak for himself and hears his full defense and testimony of the risen Christ.
Replies, 'Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.'
Rises with Festus and Bernice, and privately concludes that Paul 'might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar.'

funFacts: Naming-collision flag: son of Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12, above) — one of four men named Herod across this book's own scope, alongside Herod Agrippa I, Herod the Great, and Herod Antipas (the latter two indexed in Matthew), each kept as a fully separate tier or entry.

Per secular history (Josephus), not stated by Acts itself, he is also considered great-grandson of Herod the Great — flagged the same way as the Bernice/James 'brother of the Lord' relationships below, since Acts's own text never states this lineage.

Bernice, who accompanies him throughout these chapters, takes no independent action in the text and is historically identified (outside Acts itself) as his sister — not given her own entry here, since Acts does not itself state that relationship or show her acting apart from him.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references, kept out of the character list above because Acts does not differentiate their individual actions, or because a link to another named figure is genuinely uncertain from the text alone.

sanhedrinMembers4_6.note: Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, and Alexander, and as many as were of the kindred of the high priest — named as present at Peter and John's hearing but given no individual action. Naming-collision flag: the 'John' named here is a third, distinct figure from John son of Zebedee (indexed under Peter's tier) and John Mark (indexed under Barnabas's tier) — kept here rather than promoted to a character entry since the text gives him no independent action beyond being named present.

theudasAndJudasOfGalilee.note: Two failed revolutionary leaders cited by Gamaliel as historical precedent — reported speech about the past, not characters acting within Acts's own narrative.

antiochProphetsAndTeachers.note: Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen (brought up with Herod the tetrarch) — named alongside Barnabas and Saul as prophets and teachers at Antioch, with no further individual action recorded.

sonsOfSceva.note: Seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who attempt to exorcise a spirit by Paul's name and are overpowered and beaten by the possessed man; not individually named or differentiated.

alexanderOfEphesusRiot.note: A Jew put forward by the crowd during the Ephesus riot to make a defense, shouted down before he can speak — likely a different man from the Alexander named among the high priest's kindred (4:6), and not to be confused with 'Alexander the coppersmith' of 2 Timothy 4:14, which is outside Acts.

tertullus.note: A professional orator hired to present the accusation against Paul before Felix — a one-scene legal figure with no independent agency beyond the speech itself.

sosthenes.note: Ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, beaten before Gallio's judgment seat; possibly, but not confirmed by the text, the same Sosthenes named in 1 Corinthians 1:1 — flagged as uncertain, not asserted as the same person.

egyptianOf21_38.note: An unnamed Egyptian rebel leader the chief captain mistakes Paul for — a passing historical reference, not a character in the narrative.

act20TravelCompanions.note: Full verse: 'Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.' Timothy, Trophimus, and Aristarchus are each indexed individually above (under Paul's tier); Sopater, Secundus, Gaius, and Tychicus are kept here as one collective entry since the text gives none of them differentiated action beyond this listing.

gaiusNamingVariance.note: 'Gaius... of Macedonia,' seized alongside Aristarchus in the Ephesus theatre riot (19:29), and 'Gaius of Derbe,' listed in the Asia travel company (20:4), carry different location descriptors within Acts's own text — possibly two different men sharing the name. Neither has independent action beyond being named, so neither is promoted to a full character entry; flagged here as an unresolved naming variance rather than silently merged or silently ignored.

judasOfDamascus.note: 'The street which is called Straight... the house of Judas' — a pure address marker for where Saul is found praying, not an acting character; distinct from Judas Iscariot and Judas Barsabas.

judasIscariotDeathActs.note: Peter recounts Judas's betrayal and death, described here as falling headlong and bursting asunder in a field bought with the reward of iniquity — a different physical detail than Matthew 27:5's account of his hanging himself; logged descriptively as this book's own version, without attempting to reconcile the two accounts.
